tldr: We proposed a method that uses flow matching to jointly estimate simulator physical parameters, unmodeled dynamics residuals, and perception sensing errors (residual fidelity) online, immediately fine-tuning the policy in simulation when an anomaly is detected. In demanding real-world experiments deploying a wheeled robot with a broken wheel axle on snow, mud, and grass, it raised rough terrain success from 26% to 70%.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed NFC sim-to-real adaptation framework. Rather than tuning simulator physical parameters alone, it jointly infers the 'residual dynamics' (the gap with real-world behavior) and the 'residual environment' (sensing errors) in a latent space, adapting the policy on the simulator side triggered by anomaly detection.
overview:
Domain randomization (DR) is widely used in sim-to-real transfer to bridge the sim-to-real gap when applying reinforcement learning to physical robots. However, manually setting parameter ranges requires expert physics knowledge, and simulation-based inference (SBI) that infers parameters from real-world data has typically targeted only a few hand-picked parameters. Furthermore, as a fundamental issue, simulators miss real-world dynamics effects and onboard perception introduces reconstruction errors, setting an inherent limit where tuning simulator parameters alone cannot match reality.

To overcome this, the authors developed Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), which uses conditional flow matching to jointly estimate nominal simulator physical parameters (such as friction and mass) along with 'residual fidelity'—combining dynamics discrepancies between simulation and reality (residual dynamics) with map perception errors (residual environment)—online during deployment. By compressing high-dimensional observation histories and terrain maps into a latent space for inference, it achieves real-time posterior sampling.

Rather than constantly running online adaptation, the framework triggers adaptation only when an anomaly detector spots signs of performance degradation. From the inferred posterior, a 'hallucination policy' gates the spread of the sampled adaptation environments, preventing policy learning from stalling due to excessive posterior uncertainty.

In evaluations across extensive simulation experiments with five robots, as well as real-world trials using a four-wheeled mobile robot (Clearpath Jackal) deployed in an extreme failure state with a physically broken front wheel axle across indoor labs, snow, mud, and slopes, NFC achieved both high-accuracy parameter identification and terrain correction. On rough terrain, it raised task success from 26% to 70% and substantially suppressed severe vehicle vibrations (jerk).
contributions: Formulated and decoupled 'residual fidelity'—capturing simulator modeling errors (residual dynamics) and perception errors (residual environment)—alongside nominal simulator physical parameter calibration.

Combined conditional flow matching with latent space representations to enable real-time joint posterior estimation of high-dimensional physical parameters (up to 39) and high-resolution residual environments (128x128).

Built an efficient, informative adaptation framework that runs short policy fine-tuning in simulation only upon anomaly detection and modulates the exploration spread under uncertainty using a hallucination policy.
Demonstrated dramatic improvements in rough-terrain traversal performance on a real-world robot with a broken wheel axle across extreme environments including snow, mud, and wet grass.

sections.heading: Breaking the sim-to-real barrier: Why parameter calibration alone falls short
sections.summary: In reinforcement learning sim-to-real transfer, conventional domain randomization and parameter identification (SBI) cannot handle simulator modeling gaps or sensor perception errors. This work proposes NFC, which jointly infers physical parameters and residual fidelity via latent flow matching and adapts policies in simulation only when anomalies occur.
sections.details:
In sim-to-real transfer for robot control, the standard approach is zero-shot transfer of policies trained in simulation with domain randomization (DR). However, choosing DR ranges relies heavily on human expertise; setting ranges too broadly makes policies overly conservative and degrades performance.

To address this, simulation-based inference (SBI) has gained traction by inferring simulator parameters (like friction coefficients and mass) in reverse from trajectories collected on the physical robot. Nonetheless, conventional SBI faces two major hurdles:

- Simulator incompleteness and perception errors: Even high-precision physics engines cannot perfectly reproduce real-world friction characteristics and contact dynamics. Additionally, terrain maps generated from onboard sensors (such as LiDAR or cameras) contain noise and occlusions, corrupting the environmental geometry inside the simulator.
- Lack of scalability to high dimensions: Conventional kernel methods and optimization-based inference only handle a few low-dimensional parameters. They struggle with high-dimensional variables such as numerous robot joint parameters or 2D terrain elevation maps.

To tackle these challenges, the authors proposed Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC). In addition to calibrating simulator parameters, NFC decouples unmodeled physics effects ('residual dynamics') and sensing errors ('residual environment') into 'residual fidelity', estimating them jointly in a latent space online using conditional flow matching. By adapting policies on the simulator side only upon anomaly detection, it avoids hazardous exploration on the real robot while achieving fast, accurate adaptation.

sections.heading: Differences from related work: Beyond adaptive DR and handling uncertainty
sections.summary: We review existing approaches such as adaptive domain randomization (ADR), model-based RL, and robust control. NFC sets itself apart by abandoning the assumption that simulators are perfect, explicitly modeling residuals, and having the policy itself modulate posterior variance.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three main categories:

### Robust sim-to-real transfer and safe control
Many techniques enhance robustness against disturbances using adversarial training or safe reinforcement learning (Safe RL). However, these guarantees hold only 'within the anticipated disturbance bounds' and break down when facing unmodeled hardware failures like broken axles or extreme environmental shifts. Hence, an online recalibration framework in the real world is essential.

### Adaptive domain randomization (ADR) and SBI
While ADR and SBI studies (such as BayesSim) that narrow simulator parameter distributions based on real-world behavior are popular, most prior works rely on the unrealistic premise that 'the simulator can perfectly mirror reality.' Furthermore, approaches using evolutionary strategies, Bayesian optimization, or differentiable simulators incur prohibitive computational costs, making them unsuitable for online deployment. NFC fundamentally differs by explicitly modeling residual fidelity to accommodate simulator incompleteness and scaling to high-dimensional perceptual data.

### Optimistic exploration under uncertainty
'Optimism in the face of uncertainty' is a well-established principle in reinforcement learning. While prior methods (such as H-UCRL) explore optimistically within the confidence intervals of learned dynamics models, the 'hallucination policy' introduced in NFC takes a novel approach: it gates the variance (spread) of the environments sampled from the inferred parameter posterior.

sections.heading: Problem formulation and posterior inference via flow matching
sections.summary: We formulate the problem as a contextual MDP to infer the posterior over parameters and the environment from limited real-world data. To perform high-dimensional, expressive posterior inference, we adopt conditional flow matching, which allows sampling through brief numerical integration.
sections.details:
This study considers a contextual Markov Decision Process (contextual MDP) where the context $c$ comprises simulator parameters $\boldsymbol{\psi}$ and environment variables $\boldsymbol{e}$ (such as terrain geometry).

Given a real-world trajectory $\boldsymbol{\tau}$, the goal is to infer the posterior context distribution $p(c|\boldsymbol{\tau}) = p(\boldsymbol{\psi}, \boldsymbol{e}|\boldsymbol{\tau})$ consistent with that trajectory and maximize expected return over this posterior. Fitting a single 'optimal parameter $\boldsymbol{\psi}^*$' on scarce real-world data leads to overfitting; therefore, capturing the full posterior and running an ensemble of simulations is crucial.

### Adopting conditional flow matching
Because black-box simulators do not provide an explicit likelihood function, the posterior must be approximated using simulation rollouts. However, scaling conventional mixture density networks (MDNs) or kernel methods to ultra-high-dimensional data—such as physical parameters up to 39 dimensions and $128\times 128$ (16,384-dimensional) elevation maps—is difficult.

The authors therefore adopted conditional flow matching, a generative modeling technique. Along linear trajectories from standard Gaussian samples $\boldsymbol{\psi}(0)$ to target samples $\boldsymbol{\psi}(1)$, it trains a velocity field $\boldsymbol{v}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{\psi}(k), \boldsymbol{\tau}, k)$ conditioned on the observed trajectory $\boldsymbol{\tau}$. During sampling, running numerical integration (such as Euler steps) takes only a few iterations, enabling extremely fast posterior sampling within tight online time budgets.

sections.heading: NFC architecture: Decoupling residuals, latent representations, and hallucination policy
sections.summary: Real-world transitions are decomposed into a 'nominal simulator' and 'residual fidelity' (dynamics residual + environment residual). Flow matching is performed in a latent space to reduce computation, and a hallucination policy dynamically gates the uncertainty bounds during simulation adaptation.
sections.details:
### IV-A Decoupling calibration and fidelity shift
Real-world transitions are modeled as:
$$s_{t+1} = f_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}(s_t, a_t) + g_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s_t, a_t) + \epsilon$$
where $f_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}$ is the nominal simulator parameterized by $\boldsymbol{\psi}$ (e.g., mass, friction). Meanwhile, $g_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ captures the residual. Residual fidelity $\boldsymbol{\phi} = \{\Delta s_{t+1}, \Delta \boldsymbol{e}\}$ consists of the 'residual dynamics $\Delta s_{t+1}$' (state difference between simulation and reality under identical conditions) and the 'residual environment $\Delta \boldsymbol{e}$' (difference between perceived and true terrain). For a four-wheeled robot, $\boldsymbol{\psi} \in \mathbb{R}^{13}$ (wheel friction, damping, etc.), $\Delta s_{t+1} \in \mathbb{R}^{15}$ (residuals of position, velocity, and previous action), and $\Delta \boldsymbol{e} \in \mathbb{R}^{128\times 128}$ (elevation residual map).

### IV-B Sequential and latent NFC
Inferring a $128\times 128$ residual map in raw space precludes real-time execution, so latent representations are used. Using an encoder $\mathcal{H}$ composed of a causal Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) and an MLP, the latent residual fidelity is defined as the difference between embeddings of an 'ideal privileged trajectory $\boldsymbol{\tau}$' and a 'noisy observed trajectory $\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}$': $\boldsymbol{\phi}_z = \mathcal{H}(\boldsymbol{\tau}) - \mathcal{H}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}})$. Flow matching jointly infers this latent vector $\boldsymbol{\phi}_z$ and $\boldsymbol{\psi}$, which an MLP decoder $\mathcal{Z}$ reconstructs back into the original residual space.

### IV-C Variance control via hallucination policy
If simulation environments are naively sampled directly from the estimated posterior, early stages with high uncertainty yield extreme environments (e.g., near-zero friction causing slip, or excessive friction preventing movement), stalling policy fine-tuning within short adaptation windows.
To prevent this, a separate agent called the 'hallucination policy $\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathfrak{h}}$' is introduced alongside the control policy. Rather than controlling the real robot, $\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathfrak{h}}$ outputs gating factors $\boldsymbol{g} \in (0, 1]^D$ that scale the dispersion around the sample mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$. This allows the robot to autonomously make nuanced adjustments, such as maintaining wider variance for wheel friction while narrowing terrain uncertainty toward safer estimates.

### IV-D Informative adaptation protocol and anomaly detection
During nominal operation, the robot runs the pretrained policy while buffering real-world data for offline improvement. Using a two-sample test via a Siamese network classifier, it compares the nominal reference window against the current window. Only when the anomaly score exceeds a threshold $\eta$ (the 99th percentile of nominal data) does it launch parallel simulations to fine-tune the policy online.

sections.heading: Simulation experiments: Comprehensive benchmark across five robots
sections.summary: Using five robot platforms (Ant, quadruped, humanoid, drone, wheeled robot), performance was evaluated transferring from the pretraining environment (Genesis) to the evaluation environment (MuJoCo). NFC consistently outperformed existing Bayesian inference methods and model-based RL in posterior accuracy and policy return.
sections.details:
### Experimental setup
To emulate a sim-to-sim gap, pretraining was conducted in Genesis and evaluation in MuJoCo across five platforms:
- Ant (17 physical parameters)
- Quadruped (Unitree Go1, 25 physical parameters)
- Humanoid (Unitree H1, 39 physical parameters)
- Quadcopter (Ingenuity, 9 physical parameters, residual depth map)
- Jackal (Clearpath, 13 physical parameters, residual elevation map)

Two terrain types were evaluated: Flat and Rough (with uneven terrain and obstacles). Pretraining used 4,096 parallel environments, and online fine-tuning executed in just 0.2 seconds (5 Hz policy updates).

### Anomaly detection and inference accuracy
Using a threshold tuned to a 1% false positive rate (99% specificity) in Genesis, the proposed TCN-based detector distinguished nominal from anomalous states in MuJoCo with very high true positive rates (TPR), reliably flagging 96% to 100% of anomalous episodes in deployment tests.

In parameter posterior estimation accuracy (mean log-density at ground truth), NFC outperformed baselines such as BayesSim (MDN-RFF) and CMA-ES across all 10 settings (5 robots x 2 terrains). The generative expressiveness of flow matching combined with TCN feature extraction contributed significantly.

### Policy improvement comparison
Comparing normalized returns, PPO with NFC (PPO w/ NFC) achieved the top score across all settings. For example, on Jackal Rough, NFC achieved 0.82, whereas omitting residual fidelity (w/o $\Delta$Fidelity) dropped performance to 0.69, direct fine-tuning on real data alone (w/o NFC) scored 0.20, and TD-MPC2 achieved 0.41. Removing residual fidelity hurt performance across all robots, quantitatively confirming that parameter tuning alone cannot bridge the full gap.

sections.heading: Harsh real-world trials: Navigating snow, mud, and grass with a broken axle
sections.summary: Using a physical Jackal robot with a broken front-left axle, figure-8 tracking was evaluated on uneven indoor floors and outdoor snow, mud, and steep slopes. NFC accurately identified the free-spinning broken wheel dynamics, boosting traversal success from 26% to 70%.
sections.details:
### Severe hardware failure and deployment environments
Real-world trials used a Clearpath Jackal equipped with an Intel RealSense D435i, Velodyne LiDAR, and IMU, generating elevation maps onboard in real time. A severe hardware failure was induced: the front-left wheel axle was broken (Fig. F2).
Testing covered four indoor flat scenarios (different floor surfaces, loosely dragged rock loads) and three outdoor rough scenarios (wet grass and snow, snow-covered slope, forest mud and snow). Each controller was evaluated over nine runs on a 3-meter-diameter figure-8 tracking task.

### Inference results: Pinpointing the broken wheel (Fig. F3)
Examining the parameter distributions inferred from snow trajectories, NFC precisely identified that the front-left wheel damping was near zero (free-spinning without resistance under external forces), while estimating wheel friction around 0.4 matching the snow surface. In contrast, baseline posteriors (MDN and CMA-ES) were overly dispersed and failed to localize the broken wheel. Furthermore, NFC corrected and infilled incomplete elevation maps caused by onboard sensor occlusions and noise, sampling realistic terrain variations.

### Substantial real-world performance gains
Trajectory results (Table II) showed dramatic improvements:

- The baseline fine-tuning directly on real data (PPO w/o NFC) achieved only a 26% success rate on rough terrain, getting stuck in fruitless forward-and-back oscillatory cycles.
- The ablation tuning physical parameters only (PPO w/o $\Delta$Fidelity) improved success to 52%, but stalled because it ignored sensing errors and residual dynamics.
- In contrast, full NFC including residual fidelity raised rough terrain success to 70%.
- In terms of motion smoothness, while a high-frequency PID planner (Falco) and other baselines suffered from severe yaw jerk due to asymmetric single-wheel traction, NFC reduced turning jerk by 88%, achieving smooth traversal.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future work: Slow-drift tracking and policy retention
sections.summary: NFC demonstrated dramatic adaptation by jointly inferring physical parameters and residual fidelity via flow matching. However, challenges remain in detecting slow-onset changes like wear and tearing down/switching policies when returning to previous operating modes.
sections.details:
### Limitations and considerations
- Sensitivity to gradual environmental changes: Because the anomaly detector compares a reference window to the recent window, slow-moving changes—such as mechanical wear or gradual tire degradation—yield low anomaly scores and tend to be deferred to offline processing rather than online adaptation.
- Parameter identifiability: Short observation trajectories may not uniquely decouple physical parameters from residual terms; thus, physical accuracy of inferred values must be judged in tandem with downstream policy task success.
- Policy overwriting: Repeated online fine-tuning overwrites past behavior (catastrophic forgetting), preventing immediate policy recovery when returning to the clean original environment. Indexing policies by their posteriors remains an avenue for future work.

### Conclusion
Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC) introduces a paradigm shift: rather than tuning simulator physical parameters alone, it decouples and estimates 'residual fidelity' via flow matching to overcome physics engine limits and perception uncertainty. Successfully navigating snowfields and mud with a broken wheel axle provides compelling evidence that informative sim-to-real adaptation can elevate real-world robot robustness to the next level.

takeaways: Closing the sim-to-real gap solely through simulator parameter calibration is impossible; explicitly estimating unmodeled physics and sensor perception errors as 'residual fidelity' is vital.

Combining conditional flow matching with latent space representations provides a powerful tool for solving ultra-high-dimensional inverse problems (multiple parameters and high-res maps) online in seconds or sub-seconds.
Naively domain-randomizing across estimated posteriors can stall training; incorporating a gating mechanism like a hallucination policy to modulate uncertainty bounds is crucial in practice.

Rather than training online continuously, using a lightweight anomaly detector to trigger intensive adaptation inside the simulator strikes the right balance between real-robot safety and computational efficiency.
limitations: While two-sample test anomaly detectors excel at detecting sudden changes (e.g., hardware failures), they may miss low-frequency drifts like component wear or gradual surface transitions.
Short observation trajectories may not uniquely identify the decoupled physical parameters and residuals (unidentifiability).
Continuously updating the policy to adapt to current conditions overwrites previous learning, offering no recovery mechanism when returning to clean, nominal environments.
